thread.title: Here's Why Roku Stock Jumped Monday --- Then Gave Much of It Back

title: Here's Why Roku Stock Jumped Monday --- Then Gave Much of It Back
text:
Here’s Why Roku Stock Jumped Monday — Then Gave Much of It Back By Feb. 4, 2019 4:59 p.m. ET Order Reprints Courtesy of Roku Text size
Shares of streaming video company Roku jumped Monday as news reports circulated that investors deemed positive. The story, however, appears to be fairly complicated, and the stock gave back much of its gains by day’s end.
After jumping as much as 12% Monday, Roku (ticker: ROKU) finished up 4.9% Monday to $47.43. The rally was largely driven by investors digesting a story by BestAppleTV , later amplified by other media, suggesting that Comcast (CMCSA) won’t develop an Apple TV (AAPL) app, focusing instead on technology licensed from Roku to spread streaming TV to its cable subscribers.
Roku is looking to become less a device maker and more a company that is paid when people buy premium content through its software, view ads on content it streams, or license its technology. (First-quarter 2018 was the first time it booked more platform than player revenue.)
So, any notion that Roku might become increasingly important to Comcast’s streaming efforts surely appealed to its shareholders. (Roku also announced an executive appointment on Monday. The company’s fourth-quarter results are due on Feb. 21 after the market’s close .) Newsletter Sign-up
But investors should handle this latest Comcast angle with care. Comcast executives did suggest last year that the European Now TV platform they obtained when they acquired Sky — Roku powers Now TV —offered a readily scalable option for building digital ad inventory on streamed content.
And Comcast told Barron’s Monday that, indeed, no new decision had been made with respect to bringing its Xfinity Stream app to Apple TV. “At this time, we have not reached terms with Apple to bring our Xfinity Stream app to Apple TV devices,” a spokeswoman said. That doesn’t preclude such a deal from happening , naturally.
(Apple didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment; Roku declined to discuss its share price move.)
Comcast, meanwhile, already has its own platform, X1 , that its customers can use to access a range of content providers, including Amazon.com (AMZN) Prime Video, Alphabet’s (GOOGL) YouTube, and Netflix (AMZN). It wasn’t cheap to build, and isn’t likely going anywhere—even as Comcast routinely partners with other device makers to make the content it aggregate as widely available to subscribers as possible.
“While more than two-thirds of our Xfinity TV customers have X1 today, we also provide our customers choice and flexibility in accessing their video subscription on their owned devices,” a Comcast statement provided to Barron’s read.
There’s no doubt that there could be good news for Roku in here. But as the shares jumped Monday, investors seem to have determined that things weren’t so clear-cut.
